summary: Presents models and strategies for evolving an MPLS-TE control plane into a GMPLS control plane. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A guide for moving a network from older traffic-engineering controls to newer ones, step by step, without breaking things.

subtitle: A framework for upgrading network control planes from MPLS-TE to GMPLS.

tldr.problem: Network operators running MPLS Traffic Engineering (MPLS-TE) want to upgrade to Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) to gain new features and support non-packet-switching technologies, but cannot simply replace everything at once because their networks need to continue operating during the transition.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes three migration models (Island, Integrated, and Phased) and outlines migration strategies and toolkit approaches for managing coexistence of MPLS-TE and GMPLS devices. It covers interworking scenarios, routing and signaling interoperability, and network layering techniques.
tldr.outcome: Network operators have a structured framework to plan and execute controlled migrations from MPLS-TE to GMPLS, minimizing disruption while gradually adopting new capabilities.

facts.label: Interworking techniques
facts.value: Layered networks, routing interworking, signaling interworking, PCE

today: RFC 5145 is Informational and remains a reference framework for network operators planning MPLS-TE to GMPLS migrations. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Migrate from MPLS-TE to GMPLS
sections.content:
MPLS Traffic Engineering (MPLS-TE) provides a control plane for setting up Label Switched Paths (LSPs) in packet-switching networks, allowing traffic to be routed along explicitly chosen paths for better resource utilization and traffic engineering. However, GMPLS (Generalized MPLS) extends these capabilities to work with multiple types of networks beyond packets—such as time-division multiplexing (TDM) and optical switching—and adds new features like bidirectional LSPs, support for additional switching types, and better extensibility.

Service providers migrate to GMPLS to add new features, control lower-layer optical and TDM networks with a unified control plane, build integrated networks that span multiple technologies, or interoperate with vendors offering GMPLS-only equipment. The challenge: MPLS-TE and GMPLS use different signaling and routing protocols, so they cannot simply coexist without coordination. Migration requires careful planning to keep the network operational during the transition.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS-TE is like an old phone system. GMPLS is a better system that also controls optical networks and has more features. But you can't flip a switch—you have to change the system step by step while keeping calls working.

sections.title: Three Migration Models
sections.content:
The RFC describes three reference models for migration, each suited to different network topologies and deployment strategies.

The Island Model introduces 'islands' of GMPLS-capable nodes into a sea of MPLS-TE devices (or vice versa). Islands might be new GMPLS nodes or upgraded existing nodes. As time passes, more MPLS devices are upgraded or replaced to create new GMPLS islands or extend existing ones, until the entire network is GMPLS-capable. This model suits networks where upgrades happen in phases by geography or business unit. Within the island model, interworking depends on whether islands are packet-switching capable (PSC) or non-PSC (optical or TDM). Label Switched Paths may traverse from MPLS through GMPLS islands and back to MPLS again, requiring careful handling at island boundaries.

The Integrated Model introduces dual-capable devices that support both MPLS and GMPLS protocols, rather than replacing devices. Legacy MPLS-only nodes coexist with new MPLS/GMPLS devices. Services using only GMPLS-capable nodes can take advantage of new GMPLS features, while services that must traverse legacy MPLS nodes continue to use MPLS protocols. This model is smoother but requires dual-protocol devices.

The Phased Model gradually introduces new GMPLS protocol elements and objects into the MPLS network, creating 'hybrid' LSRs that support subsets of both protocols. This allows rapid adoption of specific features without full GMPLS implementation. However, it complicates interoperability because different vendors might implement different subsets, and all network operators must agree on which features are included.
sections.plainLanguage: Island Model: Build GMPLS zones inside your MPLS network, then expand them until everything is GMPLS. Integrated Model: Buy devices that speak both languages and let them work with old devices. Phased Model: Slowly teach the old network new features, one at a time.

sections.title: Interworking Techniques
sections.content:
During migration, MPLS and GMPLS devices must interwork. The RFC outlines four main approaches.

Layered Networks use a multi-layer architecture to separate MPLS and GMPLS control plane domains. The GMPLS architecture defines three models: the peer model, where all nodes run the same routing instance and routing information flows across protocol boundaries (requires parameter mapping); the overlay model, where MPLS and GMPLS routing are strictly separated with control plane connectivity set up separately; and the augmented model, which allows limited routing exchange from lower to higher layers with filtering and aggregation. The border peer architecture is a variation of the augmented model suited to MPLS-GMPLS-MPLS island migrations.

Routing Interworking handles how routing advertisements are shared. In the direct distribution approach, MPLS flooding of GMPLS-extended routing information works because MPLS routers simply ignore unknown extensions. In protocol mapping, routing advertisements are converted between MPLS and GMPLS formats, but this is NOT RECOMMENDED due to risk of confusion. Ships in the night uses separate routing protocol instances for MPLS and GMPLS, suitable for the integrated model.

Signaling Interworking is the principal concern. Tunneling and stitching mechanisms transport signaling transparently across islands without protocol conversion. Protocol mapping converts MPLS signaling to GMPLS and vice versa, suitable for unbalanced islands but complex in multiple-island networks. Ships in the night allows MPLS and GMPLS LSRs to use their respective signaling protocols without conversion.

Path Computation can be facilitated by a dedicated Path Computation Element (PCE) that computes paths across multiple layers or protocol domains.
sections.plainLanguage: When MPLS and GMPLS networks touch, they need to understand each other. You can tunnel traffic through without translation, translate between them at borders, keep them completely separate but connected, or use a smart computer to find good paths across both types.

sections.title: Migration Strategies and Considerations
sections.content:
An appropriate migration strategy depends on the service provider's network deployment plan, customer demand, existing equipment, operational policy, and vendor support. For packet-switching networks, the choice is between the three models above, with decisions based on the final objective (full GMPLS capability, partial upgrade, or no change to IP/MPLS) and the pace of upgrade (immediate, phased, or staged).

When a non-PSC network (optical or TDM) sits below a PSC network, two basic strategies exist: upgrade the non-PSC network to GMPLS first, then migrate the PSC network; or migrate the PSC network first, then the non-PSC network. The migration models and strategies are not mutually exclusive—different parts of the network can use different models, and various combinations may arise during the transition.

The RFC emphasizes that although interim mixed-protocol situations may exist for long periods, the ultimate objective is a fully GMPLS network where all devices support GMPLS protocols and the migration interim situations are no longer necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: The right migration path depends on your network, your customers, your equipment, and how fast you want to move. You can build new islands, use dual devices, or phased features. You might even do different strategies in different parts of the network.

sections.title: Operational and Manageability Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC includes a section on manageability considerations critical to real-world migrations. These cover control of functions and operational policies during the transition, the need for compatible information and data models between MPLS and GMPLS management systems, liveness detection and monitoring mechanisms that work across protocol boundaries, verification of correct operation in mixed networks, and requirements on other protocols and functional components to support coexistence.

The RFC also discusses the impact on network operation, including monitoring, troubleshooting, performance verification, and the need for clear operational policies about which parts of the network use which protocols at any given time. These manageability aspects are often overlooked in technical planning but are essential to a successful migration in production networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Running both protocols at once means you need to check both systems are healthy, fix problems in both, and manage policies for which part uses which. The document explains what's needed to run a stable mixed network.

sections.title: Security and Stability
sections.content:
The RFC identifies security considerations: during migration, devices from different vendors and eras are in the same network, and mistakes in interworking configuration could lead to traffic misrouting or resource exhaustion. Signaling protocol differences must not allow an attacker to exploit inconsistencies. The document emphasizes that the transition mechanisms used must provide consistent operation of new GMPLS networks while minimizing impact on existing MPLS-TE networks.

The RFC notes that MPLS-TE and GMPLS protocols can coexist as 'ships in the night' without any interworking issues if they use separate routing and signaling instances—the safest option when operational policy allows it. This approach avoids protocol conversion complexity and the associated risks, though it requires more duplication of infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: Mixing old and new protocols can create hidden bugs if not done carefully. The safest approach is to run both protocols in parallel without trying to make them talk to each other directly, until the old one can be shut down.
